claim: Ll.LtrB is a group II intron residing in a relaxase gene on a conjugative plasmid from Lactococcus lactis
source: Here, we demonstrate that Ll.LtrB, the group II intron residing in a relaxase gene on a conjugative plasmid from Lactococcus lactis, inhibits its host gene expression and restrains the naturally cohabiting mobile element from conjugative horizontal transfer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, establishing the identity and location of the intron being studied.

claim: Ll.LtrB inhibits its host gene expression
source: Here, we demonstrate that Ll.LtrB, the group II intron residing in a relaxase gene on a conjugative plasmid from Lactococcus lactis, inhibits its host gene expression and restrains the naturally cohabiting mobile element from conjugative horizontal transfer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figures 1-2.

claim: Ll.LtrB restrains the naturally cohabiting mobile element from conjugative horizontal transfer
source: Here, we demonstrate that Ll.LtrB, the group II intron residing in a relaxase gene on a conjugative plasmid from Lactococcus lactis, inhibits its host gene expression and restrains the naturally cohabiting mobile element from conjugative horizontal transfer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through conjugation assays in Figure 3.

claim: Reduction in gene expression by Ll.LtrB is mainly at the mRNA level
source: We show that reduction in gene expression is mainly at the mRNA level, and results from the interaction between exon-binding sequences (EBSs) in the intron and intron-binding sequences (IBSs) in the mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Reduction in gene expression results from the interaction between exon-binding sequences (EBSs) in the intron and intron-binding sequences (IBSs) in the mRNA
source: We show that reduction in gene expression is mainly at the mRNA level, and results from the interaction between exon-binding sequences (EBSs) in the intron and intron-binding sequences (IBSs) in the mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through mutational analysis in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: The spliced intron targets the relaxase mRNA and reopens ligated exons, causing major mRNA loss
source: The spliced intron targets the relaxase mRNA and reopens ligated exons, causing major mRNA loss.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figures 6-7.

claim: Group II introns are ribozymes that self-splice from pre-mRNA transcripts independent of protein catalysis
source: Group II introns, which are found in bacterial and organellar genomes, are ribozymes that self-splice from pre-mRNA transcripts independent of protein catalysis (Lambowitz and Belfort, 2015; Lambowitz and Zimmerly, 2011; Zimmerly and Semper, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: Splicing of group II introns occurs by the same pathway as that of spliceosomal introns
source: Splicing of group II introns occurs by the same pathway as that of spliceosomal introns, of which group II introns are the presumed ancestors (Lambowitz and Belfort, 2015; Novikova and Belfort, 2017; Zimmerly and Semper, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: Group II introns are the presumed ancestors of spliceosomal introns
source: Splicing of group II introns occurs by the same pathway as that of spliceosomal introns, of which group II introns are the presumed ancestors (Lambowitz and Belfort, 2015; Novikova and Belfort, 2017; Zimmerly and Semper, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: Group II introns are mobile retroelements that transpose into DNA via an RNA intermediate
source: Group II introns are also mobile retroelements that transpose into DNA via an RNA intermediate (Lambowitz and Zimmerly, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a reference.

claim: Both splicing and retromobility of group II introns in vivo require an intron-encoded protein (IEP) that is in complex with the intron
source: Both splicing and retromobility of group II introns in vivo require an intron-encoded protein (IEP) that is in complex with the intron (Matsuura et al., 2001; Matsuura et al., 1997; Qu et al., 2016; Wank et al., 1999; Zimmerly et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: Group II introns have a highly conserved RNA structure consisting of six domains
source: Group II introns have a highly conserved RNA structure consisting of six domains (Qu et al., 2016; Robart et al., 2014; Toor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: The largest domain, DI, contains the exon-binding sequences (EBS), which interact through base pairing with the intron-binding sequences (IBS) in the RNA exons or DNA homing target
source: The largest domain, DI, contains the exon-binding sequences (EBS), which interact through base pairing with the intron-binding sequences (IBS) in the RNA exons or DNA homing target, to define the sites for splicing and retromobility of the intron, respectively (Lambowitz and Zimmerly, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a reference.

claim: EBS-IBS interactions define the sites for splicing and retromobility of the intron
source: The largest domain, DI, contains the exon-binding sequences (EBS), which interact through base pairing with the intron-binding sequences (IBS) in the RNA exons or DNA homing target, to define the sites for splicing and retromobility of the intron, respectively (Lambowitz and Zimmerly, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a reference.

claim: DV is structurally the most conserved domain, which contains the 'catalytic triad', nucleotide residues critical for catalysis
source: DV is structurally the most conserved domain, which contains the 'catalytic triad', nucleotide residues critical for catalysis (Qu et al., 2016; Robart et al., 2014; Toor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: DVI has a bulged adenosine, which is the nucleophile that initiates the splicing reaction, yielding the branch-point of an intron lariat resulting from splicing
source: DVI has a bulged adenosine, which is the nucleophile that initiates the splicing reaction, yielding the branch-point of an intron lariat resulting from splicing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about group II intron structure and function.

claim: DIV often accommodates an open reading frame (ORF) encoding the IEP, which is a reverse transcriptase (RT) with maturase activity
source: DIV often accommodates an open reading frame (ORF) encoding the IEP, which is a reverse transcriptase (RT) with maturase activity that facilitates intron splicing (Matsuura et al., 2001; Matsuura et al., 1997; Wank et al., 1999; Zimmerly et al., 1995), and can promote retromobility of the intron in combination with the DNA endonuclease activity of the IEP (Matsuura et al., 1997; Qu et al., 2016; Zimmerly et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: The IEP facilitates intron splicing
source: DIV often accommodates an open reading frame (ORF) encoding the IEP, which is a reverse transcriptase (RT) with maturase activity that facilitates intron splicing (Matsuura et al., 2001; Matsuura et al., 1997; Wank et al., 1999; Zimmerly et al., 1995), and can promote retromobility of the intron in combination with the DNA endonuclease activity of the IEP (Matsuura et al., 1997; Qu et al., 2016; Zimmerly et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: The IEP can promote retromobility of the intron in combination with the DNA endonuclease activity
source: DIV often accommodates an open reading frame (ORF) encoding the IEP, which is a reverse transcriptase (RT) with maturase activity that facilitates intron splicing (Matsuura et al., 2001; Matsuura et al., 1997; Wank et al., 1999; Zimmerly et al., 1995), and can promote retromobility of the intron in combination with the DNA endonuclease activity of the IEP (Matsuura et al., 1997; Qu et al., 2016; Zimmerly et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: Only about one quarter of sequenced bacterial genomes contain group II introns
source: Only about one quarter of sequenced bacterial genomes contain group II introns and they are usually present in small numbers within one genome.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of group II introns in bacteria.

claim: Group II introns are usually present in small numbers within one genome
source: Only about one quarter of sequenced bacterial genomes contain group II introns and they are usually present in small numbers within one genome.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of group II introns in bacteria.

claim: Group II introns are mostly located in intergenic regions or non-conserved genes that are rarely essential
source: Moreover, they are mostly located in intergenic regions or non-conserved genes that are rarely essential.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of group II introns in bacteria.

claim: Bacterial group II introns frequently reside in various types of mobile DNAs, which include pathogenicity islands and virulence plasmids
source: In addition, bacterial group II introns frequently reside in various types of mobile DNAs, which include pathogenicity islands and virulence plasmids (Candales et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2003; Toro and Martínez-Abarca, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: The distribution of bacterial group II introns suggests that they might be deleterious to host gene expression
source: This distribution suggests that bacterial group II introns might be deleterious to host gene expression (Dai and Zimmerly, 2002a; Zimmerly and Semper, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on distribution patterns, cited from references.

claim: Organellar introns are distributed more densely in mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes
source: In contrast, organellar introns are distributed more densely in mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes, and are almost exclusively in essential housekeeping genes.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of organellar group II introns.

claim: Organellar group II introns are almost exclusively in essential housekeeping genes
source: In contrast, organellar introns are distributed more densely in mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes, and are almost exclusively in essential housekeeping genes.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of organellar group II introns.

claim: Group II introns are absent in eukaryotic nuclear genomes
source: In addition, group II introns are absent in eukaryotic nuclear genomes although they are ancestrally closely related to spliceosomal introns (Lambowitz and Belfort, 2015; Novikova and Belfort, 2017; Zimmerly and Semper, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: The relaxase mRNA abundance was much lower in the presence of the intron than in its absence (21% vs. 100%)
source: Northern blotting analysis of RNA (Figure 1B) indicated that the relaxase mRNA abundance was much lower in the presence of the intron than in its absence (21% vs. 100%).
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by Northern blotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The LtrB relaxase accumulated to lower levels in the Int+ cell (36% vs. 100%)
source: Consistent with the mRNA difference, the LtrB relaxase determined by Western blotting also accumulated to lower levels in the Int+ cell (Figure 1C, 36% vs. 100%).
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A previous study showed an even larger (20-fold) difference in protein levels in Int- versus Int+ cells
source: Notably, a previous study showed an even larger (20-fold) difference in protein levels in Int- versus Int+ cells (Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The difference in mRNA levels between the Int+ and the Int- cells was 23-fold by qRT-PCR (4.3% vs. 100%)
source: The dramatic decrease in the ltrB relaxase mRNA level in the presence of the intron was confirmed by performing quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR). The difference in mRNA levels between the Int+ and the Int- cells was 23-fold (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, 4.3% vs. 100%).
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was only a 20% difference in the amount of cDNAs between Int- and Int+ for nascent transcripts
source: Because of the proximity of the primer to the 5′-end, we presumed that the yield of the cDNA or RT-PCR products generated was a reflection of transcription initiation, and indeed there was only a 20% difference in the amount of cDNAs between Int- and Int+ (Figure 1—figure supplements 1A, 100% vs. 79%; 1B, 100% vs. 74%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reverse transcription and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The splicing efficiency of the Ll.LtrB intron ranged from 63% to 91%
source: When the intron splicing efficiency was defined as the ratio of spliced intron against the sum of the intron-containing RNAs (pre-mRNA + Intron), the numbers ranged from 63% to 91% (Figure 1B, 91%; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, 73.8%; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, 63%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple experimental approaches shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: The decay rate of spliced mRNA for the Int+ cells was ¼ to ½ of the rate for the mRNA of the Int- cells
source: Surprisingly, the decay rate of spliced mRNA for the Int+ cells was ¼ to ½ of the rate for the mRNA of the Int- cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rifampicin treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was only a marginal difference in mRNAs enriched in the polysomal fractions between Int-/Int+ cells (100% vs. 85%)
source: Comparison of mRNA polysome profiling showed that there was only a marginal difference in mRNAs enriched in the polysomal fractions between Int-/Int+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, 100% vs. 85%), thereby rendering unlikely the possibility that the spliced mRNA experienced translational repression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The differential expression levels between Int+ and Int- genes were not influenced by stressors and environmental changes, such as temperature, pH, salt and redox
source: Additionally, although ltrB RNA levels can be condition-dependent (Chen et al., 2005), the differential expression levels between Int+ and Int- genes were not influenced by stressors and environmental changes, such as temperature, pH, salt and redox (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations (data not shown).

claim: The group II intron-promoted inhibition in gene expression is likely to be mainly at the mRNA level
source: Taken together, we concluded that the group II intron-promoted inhibition in gene expression is likely to be mainly at the mRNA level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Group II intron-promoted inhibition was independent of the plasmid and promoter from which the ltrB relaxase gene was expressed
source: When the Int-/Int+ ltrB genes were expressed from different plasmids, including pDL278 and pAMJ328, where gene expression was driven by either constitutive or pH-inducible promoters, respectively, we observed similar levels of mRNA reduction in the presence of the intron (pDL: 100% vs. 28%; pAMJ: 100% vs. 45%) (Figure 2A). This demonstrates that group II intron-promoted inhibition was independent of the plasmid and promoter from which the ltrB relaxase gene was expressed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A using different plasmids and promoters.

claim: EcI5 and BhI1 group II introns cause reduced expression of mRNA
source: In addition, we extended this comparative study to other types of bacterial group II introns, including a typical IIB intron, EcI5 (Dai and Zimmerly, 2002b) and a IIC intron, BhI1 (Candales et al., 2012). The Int-/Int+ constructs of these introns were fused to an enhanced GFP reporter at the N-terminus. When expressed in Escherichia coli, levels of the mRNA dropped substantially for both EcI5 and BhI1 in the presence of the intron (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Inhibiting gene expression in bacteria is a common property of group II introns
source: Therefore, it appears that inhibiting gene expression in bacteria is a common property of group II introns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data showing mRNA reduction for multiple group II introns (Ll.LtrB, EcI5, BhI1).

claim: The conjugation frequency of the Int+ donor was 3- to 4-fold lower than that of the Int-, at 2.0 ± 0.1 × 10−4 versus 7.3 ± 10−4 exconjugants per donor
source: Consistent with the LtrB relaxase protein levels (Figure 1C), the conjugation frequency of the Int+ donor was 3- to 4-fold lower that of the Int-, at 2.0 ± 0.1 × 10−4 versus 7.3 ± 10−4 exconjugants per donor (n = 2, p<0.05) (Figure 3 and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by conjugation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The first crystal structure of a group II intron lariat has revealed that ligated exons (mRNA) remain bound to the spliced intron RNA
source: The first crystal structure of a group II intron lariat has revealed that ligated exons (mRNA) remain bound to the spliced intron RNA (Robart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from a previous structural study.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the Ll.LtrB group II intron-IEP complex shows that after splicing the mRNA is retained within the ribonucleoprotein (RNP)
source: The recently determined cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the Ll.LtrB group II intron-IEP complex, that was isolated from its native host, also shows that after splicing the mRNA is retained within the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) (Qu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a previous structural study.

claim: The small mRNA (smRNA) generated from splicing of the aptamer-containing pre-mRNA was co-isolated with the intron in pull-down assays
source: With the aptamer-containing intron, we observed that while the full-length pre-mRNA and spliced intron were pulled down as expected, the small mRNA (smRNA), generated from splicing of the aptamer-containing pre-mRNA with small exons (S-smRNA), was co-isolated. However, the smRNA produced either from the Int- cell (C-smRNA) or from the aptamer-free Int+ cell (S-smRNA) were not co-isolated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The intron is interacting with the spliced mRNA in the bacterial cell
source: These results demonstrate that the intron is interacting with the spliced mRNA in the bacterial cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The level of relaxase mRNA dramatically dropped in the presence of the intron in the trans-expression system (21% vs. 100%)
source: Northern blotting analysis again showed that the level of relaxase mRNA dramatically dropped in the presence of the intron (21% vs. 100%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting data in the trans-expression system shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Strong mRNA inhibition persisted in RT and EN mutants
source: RNA analysis showed that strong mRNA inhibition still persisted in these mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), thus indicating that the inhibition of gene expression was due to the proposed RNA-RNA interaction rather than retrohoming.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting data of RT and EN mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The inhibition of gene expression was due to the proposed RNA-RNA interaction rather than retrohoming
source: RNA analysis showed that strong mRNA inhibition still persisted in these mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), thus indicating that the inhibition of gene expression was due to the proposed RNA-RNA interaction rather than retrohoming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that RT and EN mutants still show mRNA inhibition.

claim: The relaxase mRNA level was recovered in the EBS mutant strain (21% to 92%)
source: The results showed that the relaxase mRNA level was recovered in the EBS mutant strain (Figure 5C, 21% to 92%), and increased ~2-fold in the IBS mutant (Figure 5D, 24% to 45%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting data of EBS mutants shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The relaxase mRNA level increased ~2-fold in the IBS mutant (24% to 45%)
source: The results showed that the relaxase mRNA level was recovered in the EBS mutant strain (Figure 5C, 21% to 92%), and increased ~2-fold in the IBS mutant (Figure 5D, 24% to 45%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting data of IBS mutants shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Relaxase mRNA level was again reduced when the IBS mutation in the mRNA complemented the mutated EBS from the intron in the cell (down to 18%)
source: Importantly, relaxase mRNA level was again reduced when the IBS mutation in the mRNA complemented the mutated EBS from the intron in the cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, down to 18%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting data of complementary mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The intron expressed in trans is reverse splicing into the relaxase mRNA
source: This was confirmed by probing a splicing-inactive catalytic triad mutant (T), which produced only this pre-mRNA band, RNA 1, and not RNAs 2–4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C,D, lane 3), and also by 5′-RACE followed by PCR amplification and sequencing of the cDNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). This result suggests that the intron expressed in trans, is reverse splicing into the relaxase mRNA (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting and RACE data shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claim: There was shuffling of exons or RNA recombination between two reverse splicing reactions that resulted in the formation of a chimeric precursor
source: With selective Northern blotting, along with 5′-RACE followed by cDNA sequencing, this RNA was identified as the unspliced intron expressed in trans, with its small 3′-exon replaced by the full-length 3′-exon of the relaxase mRNA (Figure 6A–B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). This result suggests that there was shuffling of exons or RNA recombination, possibly between two reverse splicing reactions, that resulted in the formation of a chimeric precursor (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting and RACE data shown in Figure 6B and supplementary figures.

claim: RNA 2, the chimeric intron precursor resulting from reverse splicing and RNA recombination, could be subject to forward splicing in the cell
source: Identification of RNA 3 suggested that RNA 2, the chimeric intron precursor resulting from reverse splicing and RNA recombination described above, could be subject to forward splicing in the cell (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of RNA 3 as a splicing product of RNA 2.

claim: RNA 3 appeared much more abundant than the relaxase mRNA
source: Notably, RNA 3 appeared much more abundant than the relaxase mRNA (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This is observed in Northern blotting data shown in Figure 6B and supplementary figures.

claim: A spliced exons reopening (SER) reaction occurs
source: Besides reverse splicing and its related RNA recombination, these experiments also suggested the occurrence of a spliced exons reopening (SER) reaction (Jarrell et al., 1988) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of free 5'-exon (RNA 4) in the experiments.

claim: Free 3′-exon of the relaxase mRNA was not detected either by Northern blotting or 3′-RACE
source: However, free 3′-exon of the relaxase mRNA, which should be produced simultaneously with the free 5′-exon from the SER reaction, was not detected either by Northern blotting or 3′-RACE (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, lane 7; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from Northern blotting and RACE experiments shown in Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claim: Bacterial mRNAs usually have a triphosphate at the 5′ end that is more resistant to mRNA decay than monophosphate
source: This could be attributed to bacterial mRNAs usually having a triphosphate at the 5′ end that is more resistant to mRNA decay than monophosphate (Celesnik et al., 2007; Schoenberg, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from references.

claim: The free 5′-exon RNA was also revealed when the intron was expressed in cis
source: Notably, this free 5′-exon RNA was also revealed when the intron was expressed in cis (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, lane 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting and RACE data shown in Figure 6C and supplementary figures.

claim: All of the identified mRNA retargeting reactions rely on the intron-mRNA interaction that is based on EBS-IBS base pairing
source: Using the in trans system, Northern blotting analyses showed that none of the four RNA products 1–4, that appeared with the wild-type strain existed in the mutants (Figure 7, lanes 3,5 versus lane 2). However, they reappeared when the EBS from the intron was mutated to complement the IBS within the relaxase mRNA in this mutant (Figure 7, lanes 6). This result confirmed that all of the identified mRNA retargeting reactions rely on the intron-mRNA interaction that is based on EBS-IBS base pairing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blotting data of EBS-IBS mutants shown in Figure 7.

claim: Group II introns are inherent and general inhibitors of gene expression
source: Taken together, we conclude that group II introns are inherent and general inhibitors of gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data showing inhibition in multiple systems (bacteria and eukaryotes) and multiple introns.

claim: Group II introns can cause gene silencing in eukaryotic cells
source: Interestingly, group II introns can also cause gene silencing in eukaryotic cells (Chalamcharla et al., 2010; Zerbato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: EBS-IBS-based intron-mRNA interactions shut down nuclear gene expression in eukaryotic cells
source: Here, EBS-IBS-based intron-mRNA interactions shut down nuclear gene expression (Qu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: Forward splicing is usually favored in the cell
source: Because forward splicing is usually favored in the cell, based on the high splicing efficiency shown in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2, we speculate that reverse splicing accounts for a relatively small portion of mRNA loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the high splicing efficiency observed in the experiments.

claim: Reverse splicing accounts for a relatively small portion of mRNA loss
source: Because forward splicing is usually favored in the cell, based on the high splicing efficiency shown in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2, we speculate that reverse splicing accounts for a relatively small portion of mRNA loss.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that forward splicing is favored.

claim: A robust SER splits the 5′-exon from the mRNA, and the free 3′-exon appears to be degraded
source: Additionally, a robust SER, which was also revealed in the in cis system (Figure 6C), splits the 5′-exon from the mRNA, and the free 3′-exon appears to be degraded (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that free 5'-exon is detected but free 3'-exon is not.

claim: RNP invasion of DNA is a relatively unfavorable event
source: However, RNP invasion of DNA is a relatively unfavorable event (Aizawa et al., 2003), which makes it tempting to speculate that the RNA SER and subsequent RNA degradation may favor DNA invasion and retromobility.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: RNA SER and subsequent RNA degradation may favor DNA invasion and retromobility
source: However, RNP invasion of DNA is a relatively unfavorable event (Aizawa et al., 2003), which makes it tempting to speculate that the RNA SER and subsequent RNA degradation may favor DNA invasion and retromobility.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that RNA targeting is more favorable than DNA targeting.

claim: The intron may act as ribosomes do on bacterial mRNA, providing a 'protective barrier' by binding the mRNA that escapes degradative attack by the group II intron
source: Alternatively, the intron may act as ribosomes do on bacterial mRNA, providing a 'protective barrier' by binding the mRNA that escapes degradative attack by the group II intron (Deana and Belasco, 2005).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to ribosome protection of mRNA, with citation.

claim: Enhanced stability may be a reflection of the reciprocal relationship between the stability and concentration of bacterial mRNAs
source: Additionally, enhanced stability may be a reflection of the reciprocal relationship between the stability and concentration of bacterial mRNAs (Nouaille et al., 2017), such that lower mRNA levels in the Int+ cell, would lead to higher stability of the mRNA.
evidence: This is speculation based on established knowledge about mRNA stability-concentration relationships, with citation.

claim: The discovery that group II introns inhibit gene expression likely explains why they are located mostly outside of genes or in non-essential genes, and why they are maintained at low frequency in bacterial genomes
source: The discovery that group II introns inhibit gene expression likely explains why they are located mostly outside of genes or in non-essential genes, and why they are maintained at low frequency in bacterial genomes (Dai and Zimmerly, 2002a; Zimmerly and Semper, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to the observed distribution patterns.

claim: Group II intron-promoted reduction of gene expression could be the major driver that selected for group II introns residing in intergenic or non-essential regions
source: Group II intron-promoted reduction of gene expression could be the major driver that selected for group II introns residing in intergenic or non-essential regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about gene expression inhibition.

claim: There are rare cases of essential genes containing group II introns in bacterial genomes
source: It is therefore intriguing that there are rare cases of essential genes containing group II introns in bacterial genomes (Candales et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2003; Dai and Zimmerly, 2002a; Zimmerly and Semper, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: In rare cases of essential genes with introns, either robust gene expression is not needed, reduction in gene expression is modest, or the intron plays a regulatory role
source: We speculate that, in these cases, either robust gene expression is not needed, that reduction in gene expression is modest or that the intron plays a regulatory role (Belfort, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about why some essential genes contain group II introns.

claim: Many organellar group II introns might have lost the ability to target mRNA and cause its loss, or do so very inefficiently
source: Perhaps many of these introns have lost the ability to target mRNA and cause its loss, or do so very inefficiently.
evidence: This is speculation about organellar group II introns.

claim: A lower expression level might be required for proper functions of organellar host genes
source: Alternatively, a lower expression level might be required for proper functions of these host genes.
evidence: This is speculation about organellar group II introns.

claim: The presence of self-splicing introns including group II introns in the mitochondrion of Saccharomyces cerevisiae was required for inefficient expression of host genes that was essential for maintaining proper mitochondrial function
source: Notably, favoring the latter notion, a recent study showed that the presence of self-splicing introns including group II introns in the mitochondrion of Saccharomyces cerevisiae was required for inefficient expression of host genes that was essential for maintaining proper mitochondrial function (Rudan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from a recent study.

claim: pRS01 promotes retromobility of the intron by providing LtrB relaxase that stimulates both the frequency and diversity of retrotransposition events with its off-target DNA nicking activity
source: A recent study indicated that pRS01 promotes retromobility of the intron by providing LtrB relaxase that stimulates both the frequency and diversity of retrotransposition (RTP) events with its off-target DNA nicking activity (Novikova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The Ll.LtrB group II intron reduces the conjugal transfer of pRS01 via inhibition of its host gene expression
source: Here our study showed that the Ll.LtrB group II intron reduces the conjugal transfer of pRS01 via inhibition of its host gene expression (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by conjugation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The two mobile genetic elements (MGEs) functionally interact by exploiting ltrB relaxase gene expression
source: Thus, these findings together suggest that the two mobile genetic elements (MGEs) functionally interact by exploiting ltrB relaxase gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about relaxase effects on both intron mobility and conjugation.

claim: Expression of conjugative transfer genes is tightly controlled to minimize the burden on the host
source: In general, expression of conjugative transfer genes is tightly controlled to minimize the burden on the host (Zatyka and Thomas, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a reference.

claim: Conjugative plasmid gene expression is kept in a default 'off' state and is switched on only under conditions that are optimal for transfer of the conjugative element
source: Indeed conjugative plasmid gene expression is kept in a default 'off' state and is switched on only under conditions that are optimal for transfer of the conjugative element (Singh and Meijer, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a reference.

claim: Silencing of the relaxase gene by its resident group II intron represents a novel way in which a conjugative element is down-regulated
source: Silencing of the relaxase gene by its resident group II intron therefore represents a novel way in which a conjugative element is down-regulated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about intron-mediated gene silencing.

claim: Progenitors of group II introns could have processed RNAs in primitive genomes
source: The demonstration that intron RNAs are not only able to transpose and cleave exogenous RNAs, but can also recombine RNAs from different sources, suggests that progenitors of group II introns could have processed RNAs in primitive genomes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed RNA processing activities of group II introns.

claim: RNA processing by group II intron progenitors could have contributed to the generation of an evolved genome and a cell that has novel functions and evolutionary advantages
source: These actions could have contributed to the generation of an evolved genome and a cell that has novel functions and evolutionary advantages.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary role of group II introns.

claim: Expression of group II introns in nuclei causes gene silencing in eukaryotic cells
source: In regard to the ancestral relationship between group II and spliceosomal introns, expression of group II introns in nuclei causes gene silencing in eukaryotic cells (Chalamcharla et al., 2010; Zerbato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: A common mechanism underlying the group II intron-promoted inhibition of gene expression in bacteria and eukaryotes is based on interactions between intron and mRNA via EBS-IBS base pairing
source: Notably, a common mechanism underlying the group II intron-promoted inhibition of gene expression in bacteria and eukaryotes is based on interactions between intron and mRNA via EBS-IBS base pairing (Qu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings in this study and cited previous work.

claim: Many spliceosomal introns are shown to enhance gene expression in plants and other organisms
source: In contrast to group II introns, many spliceosomal introns are shown to enhance gene expression in plants and other organisms (Le Hir et al., 2003; Rose, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from references.

claim: Interactions between the intron and mRNA no longer exist in the splicing of spliceosomal introns, where such pairings have been functionally substituted with interactions between U5 snRNA and mRNA
source: Interactions between the intron and mRNA no longer exist in the splicing of spliceosomal introns, where such pairings have been functionally substituted with interactions between U5 snRNA and mRNA (Hang et al., 2015; Qu et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: Through changes in intron-mRNA interactions, introns can promote mRNA levels and gene expression, or at very least not be inhibitory, and therefore provided a force that could have stimulated evolution of group II introns into spliceosomal introns in primitive nuclear genomes
source: We speculate that, through these changes, introns can promote mRNA levels and gene expression, or at very least not be inhibitory, and therefore provided a force that could have stimulated evolution of group II introns into spliceosomal introns in primitive nuclear genomes.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary forces driving the transition from group II to spliceosomal introns.
